[0] In June 2021, the National Security Department of the police arrested five former senior executives of Apple Daily and froze the assets of three Apple-related companies, after which Apple Daily ceased publication; in July of the same year, Financial Secretary Paul Chan invoked the Companies Ordinance to appoint senior accountant Tony Chan Kam-wing as inspector to investigate the affairs of Next Digital. After more than five years of investigation, the authorities announced today that there is no longer any need to continue the investigation into Next Digital and have instructed the inspector to terminate the investigation.

[1] The authorities appointed an inspector in 2021 to investigate the affairs of Next Digital. After more than five years of review, the authorities today announced the termination of the investigation. (File photo)

[2] When the authorities invoked the ordinance in 2021 to investigate Next Digital, it was the first time since 1999 that the Financial Secretary had again invoked the ordinance to appoint an inspector to investigate a Hong Kong company. The investigation covered whether Next Digital's affairs had unfairly prejudiced the interests of its members, whether there was an intent to defraud creditors of the company; whether senior management had handled company affairs for personal benefit resulting in losses to public shareholders; and whether governance was sound, among other matters. Tony Chan was originally required to submit an investigation report to the Financial Secretary within six months, but his term was subsequently extended repeatedly.

[3] More than five years on, the government announced today that the Financial Secretary, in accordance with section 845 of the Companies Ordinance, has instructed the inspector to terminate the investigation into the affairs of Next Digital, and the inspector's term of office expired on 27 July. A government spokesperson said the Financial Secretary noted that Next Digital had been ordered to be wound up by the court on 15 December 2021, that the winding-up proceedings were ongoing, that the company's listing status had been cancelled, that former senior executives of Next Digital had been convicted of endangering national security and sentenced to imprisonment, and that the three companies had been struck off the Companies Register. The Financial Secretary considered that there was no longer any need to continue the investigation into Next Digital's affairs, and therefore instructed the inspector to terminate the investigation.

[4] The authorities pointed out that, taking into account that Next Digital is undergoing winding-up, its listing status has been cancelled, its former senior executives have been convicted of endangering national security and sentenced to imprisonment, and the three companies have been struck off the Companies Register, they considered there is no longer any need to continue the investigation into Next Digital's affairs.

[5] Paul Chan: Next Digital's governance and financial issues are isolated incidents

[6] Paul Chan said that companies in Hong Kong generally uphold good corporate governance standards, and that "Next Digital's governance and financial issues, as well as the use of the company by its senior management to carry out unlawful acts, are purely isolated incidents." The authorities will ensure that Hong Kong continues to uphold a sound corporate culture and corporate governance standards, maintain a high-quality, fair and effective market, and strive to safeguard Hong Kong's position as an international financial and commercial centre.

[7] Apple Daily announced on 23 June five years ago that it would cease operations after publishing its final edition the following day. Five years after the closure, founder Jimmy Lai and a number of Apple Daily senior executives were convicted of charges including "conspiracy to collude with foreign forces." Lai was sentenced to 20 years' imprisonment; former editor-in-chief Cheung Kim-hung, former deputy publisher Chan Pui-man, former executive editor-in-chief Lam Man-chung, and former English edition executive editor-in-chief Fung Wai-kwong were each sentenced to 10 years; former columnist Yeung Ching-kee was sentenced to 7 years and 3 months; former editor-in-chief Cheung Kim-hung was sentenced to 6 years and 9 months.

[8] On 24 March this year, the Hong Kong government ordered three Apple Daily companies to be listed as "prohibited organizations"; in April, it applied to confiscate more than HK$127 million in "crime-related assets" belonging to Jimmy Lai, including bank accounts under his name and related company assets, shareholdings held by his assistant Mark Simon and his son, as well as HK$5 million bail paid in respect of the fraud case and the collusion with foreign forces case each, and HK$2 million in fines returned in connection with the fraud case.
